title: Work, Energy and Power
tagline: Work by constant and variable forces, kinetic energy, work-energy theorem, power, potential energy, conservative and non-conservative forces, and conservation of mechanical energy.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Physics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: In everyday language, work, energy and power are often used loosely, but in physics each has a precise meaning. Work is done when a force causes displacement. Energy is the ability to do work, and it comes in several forms, of which kinetic and potential energy are especially important here. Power is the rate at which work is done. This chapter connects all three ideas: work done by a force changes energy, kinetic energy is linked to speed, potential energy is linked to position, and under the right conditions the total mechanical energy is conserved.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Work by constant and variable forces; kinetic energy; work-energy theorem; power; gravitational and spring potential energy; conservative and non-conservative forces; conservation of mechanical energy

learningOutcomes: Calculate work done by a constant force when the force and displacement are not in the same direction.
Understand work by a variable force from a force-displacement graph.
State and use the work-energy theorem.
Distinguish energy from power and calculate average and instantaneous power.
Explain gravitational and spring potential energy.
Apply conservation of mechanical energy where appropriate.

learn.title: Work by constant and variable forces

blocks.text: Work is the energy transferred by a force when it causes displacement. For a constant force, work is the product of the force, the displacement and the cosine of the angle between them. That angle is important: if the force is perpendicular to the displacement, no work is done by that force. For a variable force, work is not found by multiplying one force value by the displacement; instead, it can be understood from the area under a force-displacement graph.

items: Constant force: W = F s cos theta.
If the force is perpendicular to displacement, work is zero.
Variable force: work is the area under the force-displacement graph.
Only the component of force in the direction of displacement does work.

items.text: If a person carries a bag horizontally at constant height, the upward force on the bag is perpendicular to the motion. That upward force does no work on the bag, even though the person is exerting force and using energy internally.
items.note: This is a classic point: doing work in physics is not the same as simply making an effort.

learn.title: Kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem

blocks.text: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. For a body of mass m moving with speed v, kinetic energy is 1/2 m v^2. The work-energy theorem says that the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy. This is a powerful idea because it connects force and motion with energy, and it avoids having to follow the motion step by step in every problem.

items: Kinetic energy K = 1/2 m v^2.
Net work = change in kinetic energy.
The theorem uses net work, not the work of a single force unless that is the only one.
It is especially useful when forces and displacements are known but the path details are messy.

items.text: If a car accelerates from rest and net work W is done on it, its kinetic energy increases by W. If net work is negative, the car slows down, because its kinetic energy decreases.
items.note: The work-energy theorem is about change in kinetic energy, so it is a very direct way to link force, displacement and speed.

blocks.text: Power is the rate at which work is done. Average power is work divided by time. Instantaneous power is force dot velocity when the motion is known at an instant. A machine may do the same amount of work as a person, but if it does it faster, its power is greater. So energy and power are related but not the same; energy is what is transferred or stored, while power is how quickly that happens.

items: Average power = work / time.
Instantaneous power = F.v for a moving object.
Power measures how fast energy is transferred.
A larger power does not necessarily mean more total energy, only a faster rate.

items.text: Two cranes may lift the same load through the same height, doing the same work, but if one does it faster, it delivers greater power.
items.note: Comparing power is useful when time matters, not just the total work done.

blocks.text: Potential energy is energy stored because of position or configuration. Near the Earth’s surface, gravitational potential energy is mgh, where h is the height above a chosen reference level. A spring also stores potential energy when it is compressed or extended, and that energy is 1/2 k x^2. The reference level for potential energy is not absolute; only changes in potential energy matter in most problems, so choosing a convenient zero level is part of the method.

items: Gravitational potential energy near the surface: U = mgh.
Spring potential energy: U = 1/2 k x^2.
Only changes in potential energy are physically meaningful in many problems.
The reference level must be chosen and used consistently.

items.text: A book on a shelf has gravitational potential energy relative to the floor. If the floor is taken as zero height, then U = mgh measures how much energy would be released if it fell.
items.note: The numerical value of potential energy depends on the reference level, but differences in potential energy lead to the same physical conclusions.

blocks.text: A conservative force is one for which the work done depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken. Gravity near the Earth is an example. A non-conservative force is one for which work depends on the path, such as friction. When only conservative forces do work, mechanical energy is conserved: the sum of kinetic and potential energy stays constant. When non-conservative forces act, mechanical energy changes by the amount of work they do.

items: Conservative force: work depends only on endpoints.
Non-conservative force: work can depend on path.
Mechanical energy = kinetic + potential energy.
With only conservative forces, mechanical energy is conserved.
Friction is a common non-conservative force.

items.text: A pendulum swinging without friction exchanges kinetic and potential energy, but the total mechanical energy stays constant. If air resistance or friction acts, the mechanical energy slowly decreases.
items.note: Conservation of mechanical energy is a special case, not a universal rule; it applies when non-conservative work is absent or accounted for.

keyPoints: Work by a constant force is W = F s cos theta; only the force component along displacement matters.
Work by a variable force can be found from the area under a force-displacement graph.
Kinetic energy is K = 1/2 m v^2.
Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.
Power is the rate of doing work; energy and power are different ideas.
Gravitational and spring potential energies are common forms of stored energy.
Mechanical energy is conserved only when non-conservative forces do no net work.
examFocus: Before calculating work, check the angle between force and displacement; a perpendicular force does zero work, even if it is large.
When using the work-energy theorem, remember it applies to net work, not necessarily to the work of one force.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy transferred by a force over a displacement, equal to the component of force along the displacement times the displacement.
The energy of motion, 1/2 m v^2.
Stored energy due to position or configuration, such as gravitational or spring energy.
The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
A force for which work depends only on initial and final positions.
A force for which work can depend on the path taken.

questions.prompt: A force of 10 N acts at 60 degrees to the direction of motion over 4 m. The work done is:
questions.explanation: W = F s cos theta = 10 x 4 x cos 60 = 40 x 1/2 = 20 J.
questions.commonMistake: Using cos 60 = 1 or ignoring the angle altogether.

questions.prompt: Kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v is:
questions.commonMistake: Confusing kinetic energy with momentum or with m v^2.

questions.answer: The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: The theorem links net work directly to the change in 1/2 m v^2.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the work of a single force always equals the change in kinetic energy, unless that is the only force acting.

questions.prompt: Why is the upward force on a bag carried horizontally at constant height doing no work on the bag?
questions.answer: Because that force is perpendicular to the displacement, so the work done by it is zero.
questions.explanation: Work depends on the component of force along the displacement; a perpendicular force gives zero work.
questions.commonMistake: Saying no work is done because the bag is not moving, when it is moving horizontally.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg block slides down a smooth incline from a height of 5 m. Take g = 10 m/s^2. Find its speed at the bottom, assuming it starts from rest.
questions.answer: Loss in potential energy = mgh = 2 x 10 x 5 = 100 J. This becomes kinetic energy: 1/2 m v^2 = 100, so v^2 = 100 and v = 10 m/s.
questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives mgh = 1/2 m v^2, which cancels the mass and leaves v = sqrt(2gh).
questions.commonMistake: Trying to find the incline angle first when it is not needed for an energy method, or forgetting that speed does not depend on mass here.
